summary: The paper studies temperature-scaling calibration on a synthetic 3-class Gaussian-discriminant classification task with a closed-form Bayes posterior, sweeping MLP width from 2 to 256 hidden units. It reports a monotonic trend in the optimal post-hoc temperature T* from well below 1 at width 2 (underconfident, needs sharpening) to well above 1 at width>=64 (overconfident, needs softening, replicating Guo et al. 2017), crossing T*~1 near width 16. A label-smoothing ablation at widths 2 and 256 shows T* pushed below 1 at both, contradicting the framing of label smoothing as a pure overconfidence remedy. I re-ran experiment.py end-to-end and it reproduced every number in Tables 1 and 2 exactly (bit-identical to the provided run_log.txt), so the reported results are not fabricated or cherry-picked relative to the code.
strengths:
- Full reproducibility: re-running experiment.py from scratch reproduces every entry in Table 1 and Table 2 exactly (e.g., width=2 T*=0.261/0.468 -> mean 0.37 as claimed; width=64 T*=2.252/2.713 -> mean 2.48 as claimed; LS width=256 T*=0.410/0.388 -> mean 0.40 as claimed), and the code, logs, and raw JSON are all included and internally consistent with each other.
- The Bayes-ECE metric (comparing confidence to the true analytic posterior rather than binned empirical accuracy) is a clean way to sidestep the usual ECE binning-noise confound on this synthetic task, and it corroborates the same qualitative trend as the raw ECE / T* numbers, which is a genuine internal robustness check rather than a single-metric result.
- Honest, well-delineated limitations section that explicitly flags the study as small/synthetic/low-dimensional, disclaims that the exact crossover width (~16) will transfer to other settings, and states clearly what is and isn't tested (no CNNs, no real data, no dimensionality/difficulty sweep) — this matches what the paper actually shows rather than overclaiming generality of the mechanism.
weaknesses:
- Only 2 random seeds per configuration and a single fixed synthetic data-generating instance (one draw of means/variances, RNG_SEED=0); no confidence intervals, variance estimates, or significance test are reported for the central claim (e.g. width=2 T* is 0.261 and 0.468 across the two seeds — a fairly wide spread on a single 2-point sample), so 'monotonic trend' is asserted from means of n=2 rather than a statistically supported claim.
- The central claim is validated on exactly one synthetic task (D=8 Gaussian QDA, 99.2% Bayes accuracy); despite the limitations section acknowledging this, the abstract and title state the qualitative finding ('Small Neural Networks Are Underconfident, Not Overconfident') as a general, capacity-dependent phenomenon, which is a broader claim than a single controlled task with one crossover width can support — no real-data or architecture-variation experiment is run to test whether the direction (not just magnitude) of the effect generalizes.
- The label-smoothing ablation is run at only two widths (2 and 256) rather than across the full width sweep, so the claim that label smoothing 'induces underconfidence regardless of model capacity' is extrapolated from the two extremes of the range rather than demonstrated across it (the interesting middle region near the crossover, e.g. width 16, is untested).
questions:
1. With only 2 seeds, how sensitive is the crossover width (~16) to the fixed synthetic data-generating parameters (means/variances drawn with RNG_SEED=0)? Have you checked whether redrawing the class means/variances shifts the crossover substantially?
2. Why was the label-smoothing ablation restricted to widths 2 and 256 rather than the full sweep — would the middle widths (4, 16, 64) show a smooth shift in T* under label smoothing consistent with the no-LS trend, or something qualitatively different near the crossover?
3. Given that Bayes accuracy is 99.2% and models sit in the 98.6-99.2% band throughout, how much of the observed T* trend is driven by genuine capacity-dependent confidence calibration versus the specific optimization setup (fixed lr=1e-2, 80 epochs, Adam) — was a learning-rate or epoch-count sensitivity check performed?
